title: Thoughts on The Tree of Life (2011)

commenti.body:
I think it is one of the best films ever made. And I realised that as I was watching it for the first time. To be honest I think - apart from Sean Penn walking through a door in the desert ir whatever happens at the end - it doesn’t put much on the viewer. I don’t think it needs much interpretation at all. It’s easy to understand. Critical tools needed - eyes and ears.

But then again, i could be totally wrong…

I'll repost something I posted a little while ago:

I went in blind to Tree of Life when it first came out, and it blew me away. One of the best "cinema experience" films; the creation sequence took me out of myself just as Trumbull's earlier work in 2001: A Space Odyssey had done years earlier.

Thirteen years after watching, my older brother died, and the day afterwards I was spaced out not really wanting to do anything, I thought maybe watch a movie. Tree of Life came to mind because I remembered it being a slow and meditative movie about life and I felt that's what I was in the mood for.

I had forgotten that the narrative of the film revolves around a family of sons whose eldest has died, just like in my family. I sobbed harder in that film than I have ever cried at any other time in my life -- those real guttural choking sobs -- but I'm glad I watched it, and wouldn't even really say the film is "sad". It truly transcends cinema. I was sobbing at life itself.

I saw it in the theater when it was released and I really loved it. Around that time I was reading reviews and one story came up ( a bit hazy on the exact details) apparently a cinema in Italy had been showing the movie and the projectionist had been playing the 2 or 3 reels ( this was before digital ) mistakenly in the wrong order, for the first  week of the films release, and nobody had noticed at all.
Thought that was pretty funny .

I'm glad you like it, and I wish I could say the same, but I found it tedious. I suppose my expectations may have been too high going into it, as I first watched it some time after it was released and had heard only good things (including Ebert's praise). Considering my opinion of the film is the minority one, perhaps its complexity just sailed over my head. But I'll try to explain what I mean when I say that it is tedious.

My main issue is that I think that the Biblical connection is poorly done. Look, I've read the Book of Job many times and it is one of my favourites of the OT. I think it insightful to both the faithful and those without faith. But the quote from Job feels like a retroactive addition to prop up an otherwise confused narrative. I find Malick's use of it lazy, and his 'theology' in this film is, at times, all over the place. The thematic connection to certain books in the Bible just isn't fleshed out or focused enough for it to be meaningful. It's somewhat insulting to the viewer to pose what are pretty common personal-faith questions, show a bunch of cosmic and temporally vast imagery (beautiful; don't get me wrong), not really answer those questions, and then wrap it up as if you've made something grand and insightful... I know that's a big simplification, so to be more specific, I think the instances of Biblical allusion that you find interesting, I find confused. To highlight this perfectly, you shouldn't really be coming out of a two-hour film on personal faith and theology and asking *"Is the dualism between nature and grace a distinction that is theologically sound, or does it owe more to Roman Catholic tradition than to the Bible?"* That's an indictment on the extent to which this film obfuscates its message, as you're asking the wrong question. Theology isn't just the study of the written Bible (as it seems you're implying); the distinction between nature and grace is "theologically sound" *and* it owes to the Catholic tradition; I mean (along with a few other practical divergences) its at the root of the Catholic/Protestant divide. Somewhat ironically, I think this is the only theological aspect of the film that Malick is clear on (even if he doesn't realise it) as the film seems to align pretty closely with the Augustinian account (the necessity of divine grace for salvation and the healing of human nature). I wish Malick had conveyed this in a sensible way (things can be clarified without being entirely spelled out) that carried the sort of emotive weight that an existential conflict like that holds.

I could go on but hopefully you get my point. I'll just add that, as I alluded to before, I thought the cosmic and pre-historic imagery was totally superfluous. It's beautiful, and technically impressive, but I don't think it added anything to the story and it genuinely surprises me that people seem to think that this imagery somehow adds depth to the film. You mention Tarkovsky (whose films I love), and it really just feels as though Malick watched The Mirror a few times and thought, "Let me give something like that a crack". And look there's nothing wrong with doing that, but in this case I don't think it worked. 

I know I sound like I'm moaning, so instead of tearing it down, I'll try to offer something constructive. My result may be shit, but here's how I think the film could be improved simply by a reedit: start the film with a quote from Genesis about the fall, cut the 'creation' and 'evolution' sequence, cut the famous symphonies and replace with simpler pieces of music, cut scenes that aren't particularly relevant to this idea of nature/grace so that we have a theological focus, reorder the remaining scenes to make the 'structure' and what is happening somewhat more obvious so that Jack's eventual salvific journey is affecting, and boost the volume of the dialogue so that - as you say, because what is said is so important - we can actually hear it. And so that we aren't wasting what is an otherwise beautiful sequence, with the 'creation' and 'evolution' sequence, you could make a neat shorter film called '*Creation',* rename the reedited film to *Salvation*, and think of it as a sort of double feature.

But I think you summed up part of this film's appeal when you said, *"As such it's much like other works of art, whether an epic poem or an abstract painting, all of which may feel inaccessible at first,* ***and which the average person won't readily admire or enjoy.****"* You obviously enjoy this film a lot, and the way you've written about it shows that it is a meaningful film to you, and I don't want to try and change that, but to say that enjoying this film is to essentially get something that the average viewer doesn't is a bit dismissive. With art it's obviously all down to preference, and I'm at a stage now with film where I struggle to enjoy films that rely too heavily on metaphor or allegory to try and make some kind of point. For a film about man's struggle with grace, meaning, and salvation, I'd rather watch *Winter Light* ten times over then sit through *The Tree of Life* again.   
  
I think that obscurity is so often mistaken for profundity, and I suppose that is the sentiment that sums up how I feel about this film.
You get an upvote from me, because this is a very articulate, thoughtful, and useful contribution to the discussion about the film.  Thanks for posting this!

Job and the quote from Job are essential to the movie. "*Where were you when I laid the foundations of the Earth?….When the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?*". The film goes through Jack and Mother asking a similar question Job poses to God. Why did you take my brother (son) away?  I'm not sure why you think that was added retroactively when the plot of the movie comes directly from that quote. God answered that question with a question. One that Malick discusses for the rest of the film with the grace versus nature argument.
I never saw it as heaven, but as Jack coming over to the way of grace.

I see what you're seeing, and you're quite right. I'm a bit rash in suggesting its retroactive addition. I suppose what I'm trying to say is that other than the similarity in that we have somebody questioning the judgment of God during a period of suffering, I don't think that the film goes as far as it perhaps could have gone. The reason I'm drumming on about this is that when a quote like that hangs over the film, a quote from a book with such vast existential depth, you sort of hope that the film explores that, especially when its main conflict *is* between man and his relation to the divine. And again, maybe it went over my head but I just don't think that Malick plumbs that depth (in terms of how Job's experience or God's apologia could've influenced the plot or dialogue), when it seems as though he had an opportunity to do so. If the film didn't open on the quote I'd have no issue with the extent to which Malick explored ideas relating to Job; I think I simply hoped for, and expected, more theology.
Thanks man. And likewise, the only reason I responded to your post was because you articulated your appreciation of the film so well.

The Tree of Life is exhibit A for how the people you go see a film with impact the experience. I’m open to films of all kinds, but when this one came out, I went to the theater with three friends of mine at the time. Typically with this crew we’d watch Soprano reruns at home, rewatch Mean Streets or Carlito’s Way for the fifth time, and occasionally go to the theater to watch a horror movie and fuck with each other. I don’t intend to imply that they were … simple, but that’s just what our friendship was about at that time. Just dudes fucking around. 

I don’t have the slightest clue how we ended up in the Regal cinema that afternoon watching the tree of life. I think someone saw it got an A rating and we were already on our way there having not picked anything, and we just wandered in. 

About 45 minutes in, I’m feeling PANIC, realizing that THIS IS ONE OF *Those* MOVIES and there’s been like NO PLOT so far. I look over and all
My friends have just disgust on their faces, like, what the fuck is this. And I spend the next hour continuing to feel anxious waiting for the plot to begin. We walked out dumbfounded and mocking of the movie and of each other for being stupid enough to see it.

I knew there was more there but I needed to go by myself. So I did a week later, and had an incredible experience. People are weird.

I hated Tree Of Life. I felt like I was watching a three hour long Calvin Klein Eternity ad from the 1990s. There was even something vaguely blasphemous about the film for me - the hubris of Malick attempting to express God so directly. It wasn't a story, and stories are the way human beings should think about God. For me, Malick failed to achieve here what he managed so beautifully in Days Of Heaven. This earlier work contains no cosmic imagery, no empathetic dinosaurs, no metaphorical landscapes, but somehow the mystery of the universe imbues every frame.
Cheers and thanks.

I think it has to be a reference to Jack's spiritual awakening and embracing of faith, rather than a reference to the final resurrection and the eternal glory of the afterlife.  

Now that Jack has been led to see the wonder and grandeur of God, and has embraced the perspective of faith (which he shares with his mother), he finds himself in a place where relationships can be rebuilt and where tranquility can be found. 

This interpretation fits with the overall structure of the film, which begins with Jack as an adult wondering about his loss of faith: “How did I lose you? Wandered. Forgot you.”  The extended flashback to his childhood helps him recapture his faith, and this rekindled perspective of faith is where he ends up in the closing phases of the film.

This interpretation also fits with what Jack says at the outset about his mother: “How did she bear it?” She bore it by handing her son to God in faith: “I give him to you, I give you my son.”  At the end, Jack has come to same perspective of faith as his mother, and his rekindled faith enables him to find forgiveness and reconciliation with those he loves, and most importantly an inner peace.

Seeing the ending as a picture of the afterlife wouldn't fit with the way the film opens and the very deliberate structure Malick has used.

Well said! You're bang on with the *Days of Heaven* comparison. And I agree that *Tree of Life* is a vaguely blasphemous film. Malick seems to think that it is a deft Biblical allegory and also a compelling exploration of a theological conflict, but it isn't (at least not to me, and as it seems, you). The story lacks the existential depth that the film seems to 'think' it has, and it's potential message is really just obfuscated by the cosmic grandeur and Malick's attempt at playing Creator; it needs clarity and humility. And I'm really hoping he takes this approach with his Jesus film, and it isn't essentially just *The Gospel According to St. Matthew* but shot steadicam and with disparate sequences consisting of juniper trees, the Negev, and the River Jordan set to Bach.

>For a film about man's struggle with grace, meaning, and salvation, I'd rather watch *Winter Light* ten times over then sit through *The Tree of Life* again.

Just to play devil's advocate, I prefer the latter to the former because of its use of metaphor and allegory rather than the Bergman film's literal statement of its theological and existential themes in dialogue. To me, that cosmic imagery that strikes you as superfluous makes the film open to the viewer and to his or her interpretation in a way that *Winter Light* -- by being much more explicitly 'about' certain ideas -- is not. I think it's a good thing that the film raises big questions without answering them, that it creates room for the viewer's imagination to make connections and ultimately to make meaning.
